sanskrit: तदवश्यं त्वया कार्यः स सुहृत् सुहृदां वर। अकृत्वा नहि ते सिद्धिमहं पश्यामि चिन्तयन् ॥
translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.
line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.title_en: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
prasang.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
prasang.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

speaker: Ram
setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
sanskrit: अलीकं मानसं त्वेकं हृदयं दहते मम। स्वयं यन्नाह मां राजा भरतस्याभिषेचनम्॥
translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.
line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.summary: On the morning of his coronation, Ram is summoned and told by Kaikeyi that he must go into the forest for fourteen years. He agrees without anger, and is hurt only that his father could not tell him himself. He walks out showing no change of mind, already thinking of those he must comfort.
prasang.lesson: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.

ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: My Plan of Campaign, p. 208
speaker: Swami Vivekananda
setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/my_plan_of_campaign.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word

prasang.summary: He answers critics who claimed others made his American success, noting how quickly sympathy vanishes when you dare to differ. His test of truth: whatever makes you weak in body, mind or spirit, reject as poison.
prasang.lesson: Judge ideas, and habits, by whether they make you stronger.

speaker: Ram
setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
sanskrit: कहेहू तें कछु दुख घटि होई। काहि कहौं यह जान न कोई॥ तत्व प्रेम कर मम अरु तोरा। जानत प्रिया एकु मनु मोरा ॥
translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.
line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi), checked against the Awadhi text

prasang.summary: Sita, captive and threatened by Ravana, has nearly lost hope; only the guard Trijata has been kind. Hanuman drops Ram's ring from a tree, then tells her Ram's whole story. Sita says he has been her ship in a sea of separation; he gives her Ram's message that speaking of pain helps, but there is no one to tell, and asks her to wait a few days more.
prasang.lesson: When someone is near despair, a message that they are remembered can carry them.

ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to stay steady when people and wealth come and go.
sanskrit: मानसानां पुनर्योनिर्दुःखानां चित्तविभ्रमः / अनिष्टोपनिपातो वा तृतीयं नोपपद्यते
translation: Sorrow of the mind has only two sources: a confused, wandering mind, or something unwanted happening to you. There is no third.
line: Mental pain comes from two places: something you didn't want happened, or your mind is spinning. No third.
verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

speaker: Bhartrihari
setting: Closing verse of the section on steadfastness.
sanskrit: छिन्नोऽपि रोहति तरुश्चन्द्रः क्षीणोऽपि वर्धते लोके । इति विमृशन्तः सन्तः सन्तप्यन्ते न लोकेऽस्मिन् ॥
translation: A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again in the world. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented in this world.
line: A cut tree grows back; the waning moon fills again. Remembering this, the wise do not despair.
verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 87; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.87; Kosambi 1948 no. 246 (OCR match)

prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

speaker: Narada
setting: Narada gives Shuka a plain remedy for pain that cannot be fixed.
sanskrit: भैषज्यमेतद्दुःखस्य यदेतन्नानुचिन्तयेत् / चिन्त्यमानं हि न व्येति भूयश्चापि प्रवर्धते दुःखोपघाते शारीरे मानसे चाप्युपस्थिते / यस्मिन्न शक्यते कर्तुं यत्नस्तन्नानुचिन्तयेत्
translation: When pain of body or mind arrives and nothing can be done about it, do not keep thinking about it. Not dwelling on it is the medicine for sorrow; brooding does not make it leave, it only makes it grow.
line: Not dwelling on it is the medicine. Brooding doesn't make pain leave; it makes it grow.
misuse: Applies to what truly cannot be changed; where action is possible, act (see 12.338.15).
verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CCCXXXI (sacred-texts)

prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

speaker: Sita (message to Ram)
setting: Sita's message to Ram, sent through Hanuman after months held captive in Lanka.
sanskrit: स कुरुष्व महोत्साहां कृपां मयि नरर्षभ। त्वया नाथवती नाथ अनाथा इव दृश्यते॥
translation: Show me your great-hearted kindness, best of men. I have you, my protector, and yet I look like someone who has no one.
line: I have someone who is mine, and still I feel like a person with no one at all.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit

speaker: the gopis
setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
sanskrit: निसिदिन बरसत नैन हमारे। सदा रहति पावस ऋतु हम पै जब तें स्याम सिधारे॥
translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.
line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verified_with: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika Hindi meaning (scan) or Shukla 1926 glosses (Bhramargeet) + own reading of the Braj

speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
sanskrit: नीके रहियो जसुमति मैया। आवैंगे दिन चारि पाँच में हम हलधर दोउ भैया॥ जा दिन तें हम तुमतें बिछुरे काहु न कह्यो 'कन्हैया'। कबहूँ प्रात न कियो कलेवा, साँझ न पीन्हीं धैया॥
translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.
line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verified_with: Gita Press Sur-Vinay-Patrika Hindi meaning (scan) or Shukla 1926 glosses (Bhramargeet) + own reading of the Braj

speaker: Sita
setting: Alone in captivity, Sita fears Ram has forgotten her, then reassures herself.
sanskrit: दृश्यमाने भवेत् प्रीतिः सौहृदं नास्त्यदृश्यतः। नाशयन्ति कृतघ्नास्तु न रामो नाशयिष्यति॥
translation: Love lasts while someone is in sight; out of sight, affection fades. But that is the way of the ungrateful. Ram will not let it fade.
line: 'Out of sight, out of mind' is true only of the ungrateful. Real love survives distance.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.summary: Guards threaten Sita day and night. She fears Ram has forgotten her, then reminds herself that out of sight is out of mind only for the ungrateful. The guard Trijata dreams of Ram's victory, and good omens begin to appear.
prasang.lesson: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.

speaker: Kabir
setting: Kabir on love across distance.
sanskrit: जल में बसै कमोदिनी चन्दा बसै अकास। जो है जाको भावता सो ताही के पास॥
translation: The lily lives in the water and the moon lives in the sky; yet whoever is dear to someone is always near them.
line: The lily lives in water, the moon in the sky. Those we love are never far.
verified_with: own reading of the sadhukkadi; Kavitakosh bhavarth where given; cross-checked against popular readings

speaker: Bhishma
setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
sanskrit: न चाभ्युदितसायी स्यात्प्रायश्चित्ती तथा भवेत् / मातापितरमुत्थाय पूर्वमेवाभिवादयेत् / आचार्यमथवाऽप्यन्तं तथाऽऽयुर्विदन्ते महत्
translation: Don't sleep past sunrise. On rising, first greet your mother and father, and your teacher or another elder; that is how a long life is won.
line: Start the day by greeting your mother and father. Small daily respect adds up to a good life.
verified_with: Ganguli, Anusasana Parva section CIV (sacred-texts)

prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

speaker: Ram
setting: From exile, Ram sends Bharata a message about how to treat their ageing father.
sanskrit: अतिक्रान्तवया राजा मा स्मैनं व्यपरोरुधः। कुमारराज्ये जीवस्व तस्यैवाज्ञाप्रवर्तनात्॥
translation: The king has grown old; do not push him aside. Live as prince by carrying out his wishes.
line: Your father has grown old. Don't push him aside; let him still feel he leads.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.summary: The charioteer returns and delivers Ram's messages: honour our father in his old age, be kind to all three mothers including Kaikeyi. He also delivers Lakshman's furious words about their father, showing two very different ways sons respond to a parent's failure.
prasang.lesson: Even when a parent fails you, you can choose to protect their dignity.

speaker: Yudhishthira
setting: At a poisoned lake, a Yaksha quizzes Yudhishthira; his brothers' lives hang on the answers.
sanskrit: किंस्विद्गुरुतरं भूमेः किंस्विदुच्चतरं च स्वात् / किंस्विच्छीघ्रतरं वायोः किंस्विद्बहुतरं तृणात् माता गुरुतरा भूमेः खात्पितोच्चतरस्तथा / मनः शीघ्रतरं वाताच्चिन्ता बहुतरी तृणात्
translation: Yaksha: 'What is heavier than the earth? What is higher than the sky? What is faster than the wind? What is more numerous than blades of grass?' Yudhishthira: 'A mother is heavier than the earth; a father is higher than the sky; the mind is faster than the wind; worries are more numerous than blades of grass.'
line: The mind is faster than the wind, and worries outnumber the blades of grass.
verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section CCCXI (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Yaksha Prashna: the questions at the lake
prasang.summary: One by one, four Pandavas drink from a lake against a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's riddles instead, and when offered one brother's life, chooses his stepmother's son Nakula, out of fairness.
prasang.lesson: Answer life's questions with a steady mind, and let kindness outweigh advantage.

speaker: Dasharatha
setting: The heartbroken king, bound by his promise, cannot stop Ram going but begs for one more night.
sanskrit: मातरं मां च सम्पश्यन् वसेमामद्य शर्वरीम्। तर्पितः सर्वकामैस्त्वं श्वः काल्ये साधयिष्यसि ॥
translation: Stay tonight, see your mother and me. Rest, have everything you want, and set out early tomorrow.
line: Stay tonight. Let your mother and me see you. You can leave in the morning.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.title_en: One more night: Ram leaves his father
prasang.summary: The broken king begs Ram to stay one more night so his parents can see him. Ram gently refuses, saying a promise made must be kept and he will return in fourteen years. Dasharatha embraces him and collapses.
prasang.lesson: Goodbyes to ageing parents are hard; leave with love and a promise to return.

speaker: Ashtavakra
setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
sanskrit: आयासात्सकलो दुःखी नैनं जानाति कश्चन । अनेनैवोपदेशेन धन्यः प्राप्नोति निर्वृतिम् ॥
translation: Everyone is miserable from straining after things, and no one realises it. By this single teaching the fortunate one finds peace.
line: Everyone suffers from constant straining, and no one notices. Seeing this alone brings peace.
misuse: Not against effort; against the anxious straining that rides on it.
verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en

prasang.title_en: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

speaker: Seer
setting: The second birth: raising a child.
sanskrit: स यत्कुमारं जन्मनोऽग्रेऽधिभावयत्यात्मानमेव तद्भावयत्येषं लोकानां सन्तत्या । एवं सन्तता हीमे लोकास्तदस्य द्वितीयं जन्म ॥
translation: When he cares for the child from birth onward, he is caring for himself, for the continuation of these worlds; that is how they continue. That is his second birth.
line: Caring for your child, you care for yourself. Through them you are born a second time.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Ait. Ar. II.5

prasang.title_en: The three births of a person
prasang.summary: The Aitareya describes three births: conception and pregnancy, when the mother nourishes the child and must herself be nourished; birth and upbringing, when caring for the child is caring for oneself; and death, when the parent, duties done, departs and the child carries on.
prasang.lesson: Care for the one who carries and raises the child; raising children continues your life.

speaker: Shiva
setting: Shiva tells the ancestors that guiding people beats punishing them.
sanskrit: किन्त्वहो येन यत्नेन प्रजाः सर्वाः कदाचन। दण्डर्हा एवं नैव स्युः स यत्नो ज्ञानिसन्निधौ ॥
translation: But the effort by which people never come to deserve punishment at all, made in the company of the wise, is the better one.
line: Better than punishing people is helping them so they never deserve punishment.
verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly

speaker: Seer
setting: The Aitareya on the three births of a person, beginning with pregnancy.
sanskrit: तत्स्त्रिया आत्मभूयं गच्छति। यथा स्वमङ्गं तथा। तस्मादेनां न हिनस्ति । साऽस्यैतमात्मानमत्र गतं भावयति ॥ सा भावयित्री भावयितव्या भवति। तं स्त्री गर्भ बिभर्ति। सोऽग्र एव कुमारं जन्मनोऽग्रेऽधिभावयति।
translation: It becomes one with the woman, like a part of her own body, so it does not harm her. She nourishes this self of his that has come into her. She who nourishes must herself be nourished. The woman carries the child; the father cares for the child from birth onward.
line: She who nourishes the child must herself be nourished.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Ait. Ar. II.5

prasang.title_en: The three births of a person
prasang.summary: The Aitareya describes three births: conception and pregnancy, when the mother nourishes the child and must herself be nourished; birth and upbringing, when caring for the child is caring for oneself; and death, when the parent, duties done, departs and the child carries on.
prasang.lesson: Care for the one who carries and raises the child; raising children continues your life.

ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
speaker: Swami Vivekananda
setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America, on how anyone grows.
translation: Do you think you can teach even a child? You cannot. The child teaches himself. Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles. A plant grows. Do you make the plant grow? Your duty is to put a hedge round it and see that no animal eats up the plant, and there your duty ends.
line: Your duty is to afford opportunities and to remove obstacles.
misuse: Not 'leave children to it'; protecting and providing is the hedge he describes.
verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/the_ideal_of_a_universal_religion.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word

prasang.title_en: Cups, jars and buckets: the ideal of a universal religion
prasang.summary: Truth can be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, like water taking the shape of each vessel. His plan is 'Do not destroy': help if you can, never attack sincere convictions. No one can make another spiritual, just as no one makes a plant grow; we can only remove obstacles.
prasang.lesson: Let each person, and each child, grow in their own shape.

ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, LII, p. 525
speaker: Swami Vivekananda
listener: Mrs. Blodgett ('Aunt Roxy'), his hostess in Los Angeles
setting: Letter of 2 May 1900, in failing health, near the end of his second American tour.
translation: Well, dear good mother, may all blessings attend you and peace. I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me. With love to Kate,
line: I just want a bit of peace badly — pray for me.
verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_7/epistles_third_series/52_aunt_roxy.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.7.52_aunt_roxy.p6)

speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
sanskrit: सोऽहं कित्नवमातेव द्वयोरपि महामुने / नैकस्य जयमाशंसे द्वितीयस्य पराजयम्
translation: I am like the mother of two gamblers playing against each other, great sage. I cannot wish one victory without wishing the other defeat.
line: Caught between two people you love, you can't cheer for one without losing the other.
verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXXI (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasang.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

speaker: Rama
setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
sanskrit: चेतः पतति कार्येषु विहगः स्वामिषेष्विव । क्षणेन विरतिं याति बालः क्रीडनकादिव ॥
translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.
line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

speaker: Sanatkumara
setting: The next step: action rests on happiness.
sanskrit: यदा वै सुखं लभतेऽथ करोति नासुखं लब्ध्वा करोति सुखमेव लब्ध्वा करोति सुखं त्वेव विजिज्ञासितव्यमिति सुखं भगवो विजिज्ञास इति ॥
translation: When one finds happiness, one acts. No one acts without finding happiness; only by finding happiness does one act. So happiness itself must be understood. 'Sir, I wish to understand happiness.'
line: We act only when we find joy in it. Understand the joy, and action follows.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VII.22.1

prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

speaker: Ram
setting: Ram, describing the monsoon to Lakshman, draws a lesson from ponds filling up.
sanskrit: समिटि समिटि जल भरहिं तलावा। जिमि सदगुन सज्जन पहिं आवा॥ सरिता जल जलनिधि महुँ जोई। होइ अचल जिमि जिव हरि पाई ॥
translation: Water gathers bit by bit and fills the ponds, as good qualities come one by one to a good person. River water, reaching the ocean, becomes still, as a soul becomes steady on finding Hari.
line: Ponds fill drop by drop. Good qualities gather in a person the same way.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi), checked against the Awadhi text

prasang.summary: Waiting out the rains on a mountain, Ram points out lessons to Lakshman in each sight: clouds bow low when full, mountains take the rain as the steady take harsh words, small streams swagger, ponds fill drop by drop, autumn sun dries the puddles as contentment dries greed, and fish panic as the water shrinks.
prasang.lesson: Nature keeps teaching: steadiness, humility, patience, and saving for the dry season.

ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Raja-yoga, p. 89
speaker: Swami Vivekananda
setting: Notes of a class talk 'On Raja-Yoga' (CW 6).
translation: Do one thing at a time and while doing it put your whole soul into it to the exclusion of all else.
line: Do one thing at a time and while doing it put your whole soul into it to the exclusion of all else.
verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_6/notes_of_class_talks_and_lectures/on_raja-yoga.htm

speaker: Arjuna
setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाचअयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः । अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥
translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?
line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi); data tr.en compared

prasang.title_en: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

speaker: Bhartrihari
setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
sanskrit: अजानन्दाहात्म्यं पततु शलभस्तीव्रदहने स मीनोऽप्यज्ञानाद्वडिशयुतमश्नातु पिशितम् । विजानन्तोऽप्येते वयमिह विपज्जालजटिलान् न मुञ्चामः कामानहह गहनो मोहमहिमा ॥
translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!
line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 21; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.18

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The mockery of giving up pleasures
prasang.summary: Pleasures will leave us anyway; letting them go freely brings peace, being dragged from them brings torment. We are worse than the moth, because we know the flame burns.
prasang.lesson: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.

speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
sanskrit: न तृप्तिः प्रियलाभेऽस्ति तृष्णा नाद्भिः प्रशाम्यति / संप्रज्वलति सा भूयः समिद्भिरिव पावकः
translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.
line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXX (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Kashyapa and the jackal: the gift of hands
prasang.summary: A young brahmin, Kashyapa, knocked down by a rich man's chariot, wants to die in humiliation. A jackal tells him how lucky he is to have hands and a human life, and that craving grows like fire fed with wood. The jackal is Indra.
prasang.lesson: You already have what others long for. Craving is a fire that more fuel only feeds.

speaker: Yama
setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
sanskrit: श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतस्तौ सम्परीत्य विविनक्ति धीर:। श्रेयो हि धीरोऽभि प्रेयसो वृणीते प्रेयो मन्दो योगक्षेमाद् वृणीते ॥
translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.
line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.2.2

prasang.summary: Yama praises Nachiketa for choosing the good over the pleasant. He explains that both come to every person, and the wise tell them apart, while the foolish choose what is pleasant and lose their way.
prasang.lesson: Every day offers a choice between what feels good and what is good.

speaker: Manki
setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
sanskrit: काम जानामि ते मूलं संकल्पात्किल जायसे / न त्वां संकल्पयिष्यामि समूलो नभविष्यसि
translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.
line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXVII (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
prasang.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
prasang.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

speaker: Krishna
setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
sanskrit: यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः । इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.
line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi); data tr.en compared

prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

speaker: Vasishtha
setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
sanskrit: अशुभेषु समाविष्टं शुभेष्वेवावतारयेत् । प्रयत्नाच्चित्तमित्येष सर्वशास्त्रार्थसंग्रहः ॥
translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.
line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

speaker: Nidagha
setting: Nidagha on craving.
sanskrit: यां यामहं मुनिश्रेष्ठ संश्रयामि गुणश्रियम् । तां तां कृन्तति मे तृष्णा तन्त्रीमिव कुमूषिका ॥
translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.
line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verified_with: data tr.hi

prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

speaker: Rama
setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
sanskrit: किं मे राज्येन किं भोगैः कोऽहं किमिदमागतम् । यन्मिथ्यैवास्तु तन्मिथ्या कस्य नाम किमागतम् ॥
translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?
line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
misuse: Rama's question opens the teaching; it isn't the answer. Follow it with 6a.115.43 or 1.30.17.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

speaker: Ashtavakra
setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
sanskrit: भोगं कर्म समाधिं वा कुरु विज्ञ तथापि ते । चित्तं निरस्तसर्वाशमत्यर्थं रोचयिष्यति ॥
translation: Wise one, enjoy, work or meditate as you will: your mind will still long for that state where every want has dropped away.
line: Enjoy, work or meditate all you like: your heart still longs for the place where wanting stops.
verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en

prasang.title_en: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

speaker: Surya
setting: Surya tells the seven sages how people finally turn toward wisdom.
sanskrit: सुखदुःखोपभोगेन यदा निर्वेदमागतः। निष्कामत्वमवाप्नोति स्वविवेक पुरस्सरम् ॥
translation: When a person has tasted pleasure and pain until he is weary of them, he becomes discerning and reaches freedom from craving.
line: When you've tasted enough pleasure and pain to tire of both, wisdom begins.
verified_with: data tr.hi only (no English); Sanskrit read directly

speaker: Angiras
setting: The two birds, continued.
sanskrit: समाने वृक्षे पुरुषो निमग्नोऽनिशया शोचति मुह्यमानः । जुष्टं यदा पश्यत्यन्यमीशमस्य महिमानमिति वीतशोकः ॥
translation: On the same tree a person sits sunk, grieving, bewildered by his own helplessness. When he sees the other, the content lord, and his greatness, his sorrow leaves him.
line: The bird that eats grieves, lost in its helplessness. When it sees the calm one beside it, grief falls away.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.1.2

prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

speaker: Vasishtha
setting: Vasishtha defines inquiry (vichara).
sanskrit: कोऽहं कथमयं दोषः संसाराख्य उपागतः । न्यायेनेति परामर्शो विचार इति कथ्यते ॥
translation: 'Who am I? How did this trouble called worldly life come upon me?' Reflecting on this rightly is called inquiry.
line: Ask honestly: Who am I? How did I get caught in this? That questioning is inquiry.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

speaker: Krishna
setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
sanskrit: कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः । लोकसंग्रहमेवापि संपश्यन्कर्तुमर्हसि ॥
translation: Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. And looking to the welfare of the world, you too should act.
line: Janaka and others reached fulfilment through action. Keep working, if only for the good of the world.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi); data tr.en compared

prasang.title_en: Even the wise, even God, act for the world's sake
prasang.summary: The one content in the self has nothing left to gain, yet the wise, like Janaka and Krishna himself, keep working because others follow their example.
prasang.lesson: People copy what you do, not what you say; keep showing up.

speaker: Rama's attendant
setting: Rama's attendants describe the prince's withdrawal to his worried father.
sanskrit: नोदेति परिहासेषु न भोगेषु निमज्जति । न च तिष्ठति कार्येषु मौनमेवावलम्बते ॥
translation: He doesn't light up at jokes, doesn't lose himself in pleasures, doesn't stay with his work; he just keeps silent.
line: He no longer laughs at jokes, enjoys pleasures, or stays with his work. He just goes quiet.
misuse: If this describes you for weeks, talk to someone you trust or a doctor. Rama too was helped by others.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
prasang.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
prasang.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

speaker: Narada
setting: Narada, master of every science, comes to Sanatkumara.
sanskrit: सोऽहं भगवो मन्त्रविदेवास्मि नात्मविच्छ्रुतꣳ ह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्यस्तरति शोकमात्मविदिति सोऽहं भगवः शोचामि तं मा भगवाञ्छोकस्य पारं तारयत्विति तꣳ होवाच यद्वै किंचैतदध्यगीष्ठा नामैवैतत् ॥
translation: 'Sir, I know only the texts; I do not know the self. I have heard from people like you that one who knows the self crosses beyond sorrow. I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across.' He said to him: 'Whatever you have studied is only name.'
line: I have learned so much, yet I am sad. I know words, not myself. Help me cross this sorrow.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VII.1.3

prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

speaker: Manu
setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
sanskrit: जथा दरिद्र बिबुधतरु पाई। बहु संपति मागत सकुचाई॥ तासु प्रभाउ जान नहिं सोई। तथा हृदयँ मम संसय होई ॥
translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.
line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi), checked against the Awadhi text

prasang.title_en: Manu and Shatarupa ask late in life
prasang.summary: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa realise in old age that a whole life has passed without what mattered most to them. They hand over the kingdom, go to the forest and practise austerity for years. When Vishnu offers a boon, Manu hesitates like a poor man before the wishing tree, then asks for a son like God himself.
prasang.lesson: It is not too late to turn towards what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.

speaker: Vishnu
setting: Vishnu explains to the frightened gods where fear comes from.
sanskrit: दीनताजं भयं माने गुणे खलभयं खलु । भयं निन्दकजं शक्तौ विद्यायां वादिनं भयम् ॥
translation: In honour lies the fear of being brought low; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; in power, the fear of critics; in learning, the fear of rival debaters.
line: Honour fears disgrace, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, learning fears debate. Every gain brings a fear.
verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly

prasang.title_en: Vishnu on where fear comes from
prasang.summary: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He explains that every possession carries its own fear (the body fears age, wealth fears thieves, power fears critics) and that only dispassion is free of fear; then he restates Bhagavad Gita 2.14-15 on enduring pleasure and pain.
prasang.lesson: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.

speaker: Bhartrihari
setting: From the section on action.
sanskrit: कदर्थितस्यापि हि धैर्यवृत्तेर्न शक्यते धैर्यगुणः प्रमार्ष्टुम् । अधोमुखस्यापि कृतस्य वह्नेर्नाधः शिखा याति कदाचिदेव ॥
translation: Even when harassed, the steadfast cannot be robbed of their steadiness. Hold a torch upside down: its flame never points downward.
line: Turn a torch upside down and its flame still rises. Steadiness survives humiliation.
verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 106; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.105; Kosambi 1948 no. 226 (OCR match)

prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
speaker: Draupadi
setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
sanskrit: न त्वेवात्माऽवमन्तव्यः पुरुषेण कदाचन / न ह्यात्मपरिभूतस् भूतिर्भवति शोभना
translation: A person should never look down on himself. The one who despises himself never finds real prosperity.
line: Never look down on yourself. Nothing good grows from self-contempt.
verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXXII (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

speaker: Vasishtha
setting: Vasishtha tells Rama how to steer his own habits.
sanskrit: समता सांत्वनेनाशु न द्रागिति शनेशनेः । पौरुषेणैव यत्नेन पालयेच्चित्तबालकम् ॥
translation: With evenness and gentle coaxing, not in a rush but little by little, by steady effort, look after the child that is your mind.
line: Raise your mind like a child: gently, patiently, little by little, never by force.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

speaker: Nala
setting: The army is stuck at the ocean; Nala reveals he can build a bridge, which he had not mentioned.
sanskrit: समर्थश्चाप्यहं सेतुं कर्तुं वै वरुणालये। तस्मादद्यैव बध्नन्तु सेतुं वानरपुङ्गवाः॥
translation: I too am able to build a bridge across the ocean. So let the best of the monkeys start building it this very day.
line: I can build this. Let's start today.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.summary: Ram waits three days for the ocean to let him pass, then loses patience. The ocean reveals that Nala can build a bridge; Nala admits his skill and the whole army hauls trees and rocks for five days until the bridge reaches Lanka.
prasang.lesson: Big things get built by many hands, once someone admits they know how.

speaker: Sutikshna
setting: The young sage Sutikshna hears Ram is coming and runs to meet him, full of doubt about himself.
sanskrit: सहित अनुज मोहि राम गोसाईं। मिलिहहिं निज सेवक की नाईं॥ मोरे जियँ भरोस दृढ़ नाहीं। भगति बिरति न ग्यान मन माहीं ॥ नहिं सतसंग जोग जप जागा। नहिं दृढ़ चरन कमल अनुरागा॥ एक बानि करुनानिधान की। सो प्रिय जाकें गति न आन की ॥
translation: 'Will Ram, my master, with his brother, meet me as he would his own servant? There is no firm trust in my heart; no devotion, detachment or wisdom in my mind; no good company, no yoga, chanting or sacrifice, no steady love for his lotus feet. But the ocean of compassion has one habit: the one who has no other refuge is dear to him.'
line: I have no devotion, no wisdom, no steady love. But he loves the one who has nowhere else to go.
misuse: Grace doesn't erase responsibility or consequences; it means you don't carry them alone.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi) + own reading of the Awadhi

prasang.summary: A young sage hears Ram is near and runs out, sure he has no devotion, wisdom or discipline worth anything, trusting only that Ram loves those with nowhere else to go. Lost in love he wanders, dances, forgets the way; Ram watches from behind a tree, then lifts him up and holds him. Asked for a boon, the sage says only: may this one pride never leave me, that I am his.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to feel qualified; the one with nowhere else to go is the one he loves.

speaker: Savitri
setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
sanskrit: न कार्यस्तात संतापः पारयिष्याम्यहं व्रतम् / व्यसंसायकृतं हीदं व्यवसायश्च कारणम्
translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.
line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section CCXCIV (sacred-texts)

prasang.summary: Princess Savitri marries Satyavan knowing he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows Yama, the lord of death, speaking such wisdom about goodness and friendship that he grants boon after boon, until she wins back her husband's life.
prasang.lesson: Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop.

speaker: Yajnavalkya
setting: Yajnavalkya on how a person becomes what they are.
sanskrit: अथो खल्वाहुः काममय एवायं पुरुष इति स यथाकामो भवति तत्क्रतुर्भवति यत्क्रतुर्भवति तत्कर्म कुरुते यत्कर्म कुरुते तदभिसम्पद्यते ॥
translation: And so they say: a person is made of desire. As his desire is, so is his will; as his will is, so is his deed; and whatever deed he does, that he becomes.
line: As your desire, so your will; as your will, so your deeds; as your deeds, so you become.
verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.5

prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

speaker: Hanuman
setting: Having searched all of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman fights off despair.
sanskrit: अनिर्वेदः श्रियो मूलमनिर्वेदः परं सुखम्। भूयस्तत्र विचेष्यामि न यत्र विचयः कृतः॥
translation: Not losing heart is the root of success; not losing heart is the highest happiness. I will search again, in the places I have not yet searched.
line: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success. Look again where you have not yet looked.
verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit

prasang.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasang.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

speaker: Ram
setting: Vibhishan panics: Ravana has a chariot, Ram stands barefoot. Ram describes the chariot that actually wins.
sanskrit: सौरज धीरज तेहि रथ चाका। सत्य सील दृढ़ ध्वजा पताका॥ बल बिबेक दम परहित घोरे। छमा कृपा समता रजु जोरे ॥
translation: Valour and patience are the wheels of that chariot; truth and good conduct are its firm flag and banner. Strength, discernment, self-control and kindness to others are its horses, yoked with the reins of forgiveness, compassion and evenness of mind.
line: Courage and patience are the wheels; truth and character, the flag. That is the chariot that wins.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi), checked against Awadhi text

prasang.summary: Ravana rides out in a chariot; Ram stands on foot, and Vibhishan worries. Ram describes the chariot that really wins: courage and patience as its wheels, truth and character as its flag, strength, judgement, self-control and kindness as its horses.
prasang.lesson: Inner qualities are the real equipment for a hard fight.

speaker: Vasishtha
setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
sanskrit: भोक्ता तृप्यति नाभोक्ता गन्ता गच्छति नागतिः । वक्ता वक्ति न चावक्ता पौरुषं सफलं नृणाम् ॥
translation: The one who eats is satisfied, not the one who doesn't; the one who walks arrives, not the one who stays put; the one who speaks is heard, not the silent one. Human effort bears fruit.
line: The eater gets full, the walker arrives, the speaker is heard. Effort is what bears fruit.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

speaker: Bhartrihari
setting: Opening verse of the section on steadfastness, recalling the churning of the ocean.
sanskrit: रत्नैर्महार्हैस्तुतुषुर्न देवा न भेजिरे भीमविषेण भीतिम् । सुधां विना न प्रययुर्विरामं न निश्चितार्थाद्विरमन्ति धीराः ॥
translation: The gods were not satisfied by priceless jewels, nor frightened off by the terrible poison; they did not rest until they had the nectar. The steadfast do not stop short of what they have set out to do.
line: The gods churned past jewels and past poison until they reached nectar. The steady don't stop halfway.
misuse: Steadiness is not refusing to reassess a goal.
verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 80; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.81; Kosambi 1948 no. 52 (OCR match)

prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XLVII, p. 91
speaker: Swami Vivekananda
setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.
line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.
verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_5/epistles_first_series/047_maharaja_of_khetri.htm

prasang.summary: Facing opposition from some clergy in America, he writes to his friend the Maharaja that every work passes through ridicule, opposition and then acceptance. Anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood, so he will stay steady.
prasang.lesson: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

speaker: Krishna
setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
sanskrit: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥
translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.
line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi); data tr.en compared

prasang.summary: Krishna praises knowledge: learn it humbly from those who know, it carries even the worst wrongdoer across, faith and self-control bring it, and doubt destroys. He ends: cut your doubt and stand up.
prasang.lesson: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

speaker: Rama
setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
sanskrit: संसारदुःखपाषाणनीरन्ध्रहृदयोऽप्यहम् । निजलोकभयादेव गलद्वाष्पं न रोदिमि ॥
translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.
line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
misuse: Holding tears in is not strength. Rama's healing began when he finally said it aloud.
verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

speaker: Vibhishan
setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
sanskrit: सुनहु पवनसुत रहनि हमारी। जिमि दसनन्हि महुँ जीभ बिचारी॥ तात कबहुँ मोहि जानि अनाथा। करिहहिं कृपा भानुकुल नाथा ॥
translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?
line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi), checked against the Awadhi text

prasang.title_en: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
prasang.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
prasang.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

speaker: Vidura
setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
sanskrit: न तन्मित्रं यस्य कोपाद्बिभेति / यद्वा मित्रं शङ्कितेनोपचर्यम् / यस्मिन्मित्रे पितरीवाश्वसीत / तद्वै मित्रं सङ्गतानीतराणि
translation: That is no friend whose anger you fear, or whom you must approach warily. A friend is one you can trust as you trust a father; the rest are mere acquaintances.
line: If you fear someone's anger or must tiptoe around them, they are not really your friend.
verified_with: Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section XXXVI (sacred-texts)

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: Atreya and the Sadhyas, on insult and anger
prasang.summary: Vidura retells the sage Atreya's answer to the gods: don't insult back, hold your tongue, choose your company. He adds that anger is a bitter drink and that kin who stand together survive storms.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, don't insult back. Swallow anger, and stand with your own people.

speaker: Ram
setting: Ram, having embraced Vibhishan, asks how he survived in Lanka.
sanskrit: खल मंडली बसहु दिनु राती। सखा धरम निबहइ केहि भाँती॥ मैं जानउँ तुम्हारि सब रीती। अति नय निपुन न भाव अनीती ॥
translation: 'You lived day and night among the wicked; how did you keep your goodness, friend? I know all your ways: very wise in conduct, with no taste for wrong.'
line: You lived among the cruel day and night. I know how you kept your goodness.
verified_with: Gita Press Hindi meaning in data (tr.hi) + own reading of the Awadhi

prasang.title_en: Vibhishan crosses over: Ram's refuge speech
prasang.summary: Kicked out of Lanka for telling his brother the truth, Vibhishan crosses the sea to Ram, dreaming of his feet. Sugriva wants him bound as a spy; Ram says his vow is to remove the fear of anyone who comes for refuge, and if the visitor were truly wicked he would not have come at all. Ram embraces him, asks how he kept his goodness among the cruel, describes the devotee who ties every thread of love to him, and crowns him king, shyly giving what Ravana got for ten heads.
prasang.lesson: The turning itself is enough to be taken in; your past is not the deciding question.

speaker: Bhartrihari
setting: From the section on the wicked.
sanskrit: दुर्जनः परिहर्तव्यो विद्ययालङ्कृतोऽपि सन् । मणिना भूषितः सर्पः किमसौ न भयङ्करः ॥
translation: A wicked person should be avoided, even if adorned with learning. Is a snake any less frightening because it wears a jewel?
line: Avoid a cruel person even if brilliant. A snake wearing a jewel still bites.
misuse: It means keeping distance from people who harm you, not labelling everyone who annoys you.
verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 53; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.53

prasang.summary: A field guide to toxic people: the brilliant but cruel, the spiteful critic who turns every virtue into a fault, the boss nobody can please, and friendships that shrink like morning shade.
prasang.lesson: Recognise spite for what it is, keep your distance, and stop taking it personally.
